description: We are high school students from Bangladesh, class 9 and 10, building a climate trend detection tool on live NASA data. Climate change hits Bangladesh hard and we wanted to answer the real question: not just whether a trend exists, but when it becomes statistically confirmed and whether the data is even strong enough to detect it at all.
summary:
Most climate analysis tool answers one question: is this trend significant right now? When the answer is no, the analysis stops. tidemark answers what comes next.

For any location on Earth and any of 19 NASA-measured climate variables, tidemark runs a rigorous trend test and then projects when the trend will reach statistical significance using four independent methods. It computes a detection floor that shows whether a trend is even resolvable at the current record length. It detects structural breaks in the data with a Bayesian scan. It separates El Nino and La Nina influence from the forced trend.

A researcher who sees p = 0.07 on 45 years of Dhaka temperature data has no principled way to ask "how much longer?" tidemark gives four independent answers, an uncertainty range, and a plain explanation if the answers disagree.
details:
Source Code: https://github.com/raiyanruhan/tidemark

Whitepaper: https://tidemark.hylith.com/whitepaper.pdf

What it does and how it works

tidemark fetches data from five NASA sources: POWER (MERRA-2 reanalysis, 1981 to present), GPM IMERG (precipitation, 2001 to present), AppEEARS MODIS (land surface temperature and evapotranspiration), ORNL DAAC MODIS (vegetation index NDVI), and LAADS DAAC MODIS (aerosol optical depth, 2002 to present). Nineteen variables total. Any coordinate on Earth. No preprocessing required.

For each variable, tidemark tests significance with a Mann-Kendall test whose null distribution is bootstrapped from the series itself, so the result accounts for that series' own autocorrelation and skew. On simulated trend-free data this test raised false alarms 6 to 8% of the time, against 7 to 16% for our earlier method selection. Block bootstrap Mann-Kendall, the MKC3 third-order cumulant correction and Modified Mann-Kendall with Hamed-Rao correction are reported alongside for comparison. No configuration needed.

The significance trajectory is the main output. When a trend is not yet confirmed, tidemark projects the crossing year four ways: an analytical formula derived from the n^1.5 growth of the Mann-Kendall Z-statistic (we have not found it published in this form), the Weatherhead et al. 1998 detection time formula widely used in atmospheric science for detection-time planning, a 1000-run Monte Carlo simulation that keeps the data's autocorrelation and allows for uncertainty in the slope, and a Cramer-Rao lower bound from Fisher information theory (an estimate of the theoretical minimum). When the four estimates agree, confidence is high. When Monte Carlo diverges, tidemark measures skewness, runs a normality test, and reports the cause in plain language.

The detection floor translates statistical power into physical units per year. It tells a user whether their trend is weak or whether the data record is simply too short to resolve it, regardless of which test is used.

A trend-break test finds the year when a trend regime changed, comparing one straight line against two at every candidate split year. For Dhaka temperature, it found a 1997 break in the trend line (p = 0.006) within a trend that is significant overall (p = 0.037)

ENSO separation uses the NOAA MEI v2 index to remove El Nino and La Nina variability from the trend signal by regression, and a rank-based partial Mann-Kendall test checks whether the trend survives once ENSO is controlled for.

Benefits and intended impact

For scientists, the detection floor is a principled instrument characterization: it shows whether more data would actually help, or whether the signal-to-noise ratio of the variable is the fundamental constraint.

For planners and policymakers in water-stressed regions, island states, and dryland farming communities, knowing whether a climate signal will confirm in 2035 or 2070 is a planning-critical difference. tidemark makes that distinction quantitative and reproducible.

Factors considered

The web interface at tidemark.hylith.com runs on a cloud VPS and requires only a browser, so analysis is accessible to users without programming experience. POWER variables (temperature, humidity, soil moisture, wind) require no login, so the core analysis is accessible to anyone with an internet connection.Variables from GPM, AppEEARS and LAADS use NASA Earthdata credentials configured on the server. The CLI also runs fully on the user's own machine for users who prefer local execution. Cached results make repeated analyses of the same location instant.

Tools, languages, and frameworks

Rust (clap v4, serde) handles argument parsing and terminal output. Python 3.10 handles statistics and data fetching using numpy, scipy, pymannkendall, Flask, gunicorn, and requests. The web interface uses the Vanilla Framework with server-sent events for real-time progress.

Creativity

As far as we know, five contributions in tidemark have no prior open implementation. The analytical MK detection time formula derived from the n^1.5 Z-growth rate we have not found published in closed usable form. The Weatherhead 1998 formula, standard in NASA mission planning, we have not seen in a user-facing climate tool. The Cramer-Rao lower bound on detection time is not computed by any existing trend tool. The MKC3 variance correction (Then and Abdul Halim 2025) has no prior open Python implementation. The block bootstrap Mann-Kendall p-value (Onoz and Bayazit 2012) also has no prior open Python implementation. The four-method cross-validation with automatic divergence diagnosis produces something new: a trend report that explains why a signal is hard to confirm, not just that it is.
